newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Telefonica to abandon cable TV venture - sources.
newsitem.headline: Telefonica to abandon cable TV venture - sources.

text.p: Spanish telecoms group Telefonica de Espana is set to pull out of its cable television venture with pay TV giant Sogecable SA due to European Commission opposition, European Union sources said on Monday.
The partly state-owned Spanish telecoms operator preferred to drop out now rather than face an expected ruling against the venture by the EU executive later this month, they said.
"Telefonica has said that if the Commission comes up with a negative decision, they will withdraw the case well in advance of the decision," one EU source said.

The joint venture was set up by Telefonica and Sogecable SA, a unit of Promotora de Informaciones SA and France's Canal Plus, in July 1995 to operate and distribute pay television and multimedia in Spain via cable TV networks.
Sogecable and Canal Plus Espana, a subsidiary of the French company, are both in the fast-growing pay-television business and Telefonica is the country's dominant telecoms operator.
Ten million households have televisions in Spain but only 200,000 have access to cable, making it one of the largest untapped markets left in western Europe.
The deadline for a Commission decision on whether to clear the Cablevision venture is on November 26.
Company sources told daily El Mundo last week Telefonica's directors would recommend the dissolution of Cablevision at the next board meeting on November 11.
However, it was not clear what would happen to the venture if Telefonica, a strategic partner, decides to leave.
When it began a full probe into the case in July, the Commission expressed strong doubts about it because Telefonica still has a monopoly on the local telecommunications market.
The operation would affect the market for cable television services and would also have an indirect impact on the telephone and data transmission sectors, it said at the time.
The Commission, which vets all major corporate agreements which affect trade in the EU, has become increasingly tough on media alliances and especially on cable pay-television deals.

In 1994, the Commission blocked a German pay-TV deal between telecoms giant Deutsche Telekom and leading media companies Bertelsmann and Leo Kirch over fears it would close Europe's largest market to competition.

It banned another two operations in the media sector in 1995 -- in the Nordic area and in the Netherlands -- prompting much criticism from the industry which argues that similar deals have been cleared without trouble in the United States, giving U.S. companies a competitive edge over Europe.
Telefonica is also involved in the Unisource alliance, which still awaits Commission approval.
The Commission has said it will only approve Unisource if Spain effectively opens up its telecoms market by January 1, 1998, waiving a five-year delay.
Unisource also groups telecoms operators Dutch PTT, Telia AB of Sweden and Swiss Telecom PTT. Telefonica has 25 percent of the alliance.
